KAVACH: User Login Analysis Using LLM
KAVACH monitors login activity as it happens.
It saves the result (success or failure), time, IP address, and device.
One failed login could be a typo.
Several failures in a short time could point to password guessing.
With many login records, it is hard to know which account to check first.

KAVACH monitors login activity as it happens. It records whether a sign-in succeeded or failed, along with the time, IP address, and device. One failed login might be a typo. Several failures in a short time could point to password guessing. When there are many login records, an administrator has to sort through them to decide which account to check first.

Sign-in, personal login history, and administrator dashboard
REST API · JWT for protected requests
Check account status and verify the password with BCrypt.
Save result, time, IP, and device for known accounts.
Apply six rules and link matches to the login.
Use the last 24 hours of points and cap the score at 100.
Stores accounts, login events, anomalies, audit logs, and AI report history.
Receives alert details and returns a risk explanation and suggested checks.

Start with React. Users sign in and review their own activity. Administrators can see the dashboard and request a report. Spring Boot checks credentials with BCrypt and issues a JWT on successful login. For known accounts, the telemetry service records the result, time, IP, and device independently of the authentication transaction. The detector evaluates six rules against the saved event. When the dashboard requests risk, Spring Boot totals the last 24 hours of anomaly points and caps the score at 100. The left branch uses JPA to read and write PostgreSQL records. The right branch sends selected anomaly and linked login details to Grok in a JSON request when analysis is requested. Grok returns an explanation and recommended checks that KAVACH displays as a report.

Total risk = sum of alert points from the last 24 hours
Use alerts for the same account. No recent alerts gives a total of 0.
Take the smaller of the total risk and 100.
The dashboard counts accounts scoring 60 or above as risky.

For each account, add the points from alerts detected in the last 24 hours. Zero recent alerts means zero points. The min function takes the smaller of the total and 100. For example, 130 points becomes 100. Find the displayed score in the table to get the tier. A score of 60 or above counts as risky on the dashboard.

KAVACH: User Login Analysis Using LLM
Example · An account starts at 0 risk points
The account uses a familiar device from a new IP.

20 failed login + 25 unusual time
+ 40 new IP
All five use the same IP and device.

5 × (20 + 25) = 225 for failures and off-hours
2 × 70 = 140 for brute force
Brute force matches on failures 5 and 6 overall.

Assume the account has earlier login history, zero recent risk points, and a familiar device. At 02:15 the first failed sign-in comes from a new IP. It adds 20 for failed login, 25 for unusual time, and 40 for the new IP. That makes 85, which is already Critical. At 02:16, five more attempts from the same IP each add 45 for failed login and unusual time. Two of those attempts are the fifth and sixth failures overall, so they each add 70 for brute force. The complete raw total is 85 plus 225 plus 140, or 450. KAVACH displays 100 because of the cap.

On an alert, select Analyze with AI Engine. The backend builds a prompt from the selected anomaly and linked login details, sends it in a JSON request, and parses the structured response. The report explains the risk, indicators, possible implications, and what to check. The backend rules assign points separately.

Log collection. Bring in sign-in logs from other applications, single sign-on providers, and VPNs through live feeds or batch imports.
Account matching. Link verified accounts across systems and count each login once.
Telegram alerts. Use a bot to notify administrators of High or Critical risk and link to the KAVACH report.

Today KAVACH monitors its own website. In the future, I would collect sign-in records from other web apps, identity providers, and VPNs through live feeds or batch imports. I would match verified accounts and count each login once. A Telegram bot could notify the administrator when an account reaches High or Critical risk and include a link to the report in KAVACH.
